In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the action of albumin on aged mitochondria is due to a physical rather than to a chemical effect.
albumin does not reverse uncoupling in aged mitochondria by inactivating an uncoupling substance, and that the effect of albumin is not due to the formation of a complex with the mitochondria.

(i) the uncoupling activity is a fatty acid, (ii) the uncoupled fatty acid is not a product of oxidation of the fatty acid, (iii) the fatty acid is not released from mitochondria, and (iv) the fatty acid does not react with albumin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

albumin does not reverse uncoupling in aged mitochondria by forming complexes with the uncoupling factor, and that it is not necessary to assume that albumin has an effect on the mitochondrial membranes.
albumin restores oxidative phosphorylation by a mechanism that is not dependent on its ability to form fatty acid complexes.
the uncoupling agent formed in aged mitochondria is not inactivated by albumin, but that the albumin is able to restore phosphorylation by preventing the release of the agent from the mitochondria.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the uncoupling activity in aged mitochondria is not due to a fatty acid or any other substance formed by mitochondria in the presence of albumin.

the mechanism by which bovine serum album in (BSA) reverses the uncoupling effect of damaged mitochondria is not by the formation of an enzyme complex with the uncoupling agent, as previously postulated (3, 7-10).
the mechanism is not due to the formation of an albumin-fatty acid complex, as suggested by Lehninger and Remmer (7).
